title: The Square-Root Key: a machine for manufacturing primes

lines.text: Zeno's old puzzle. Walk half way to the wall. Then half of what is left. Then half again. Infinitely many steps, and you never pass two.
Lay the steps out as arrows: one, a half, a quarter, an eighth. The chain shrinks fast and stops dead at two.
Now a gentler rule. The second arrow is one over the square root of two. The third, one over root three. Every arrow is one over the square root of its number.
Shrinking this slowly, the chain never stops. Sixty arrows reach fourteen. A million reach two thousand. It runs off the floor forever.
Hold on to that square root. The exponent one half is the key to everything that follows, and we will come back to it at the end.

chapters.title: The Stage
chapters.subtitle: A floor, a pole, and a dial

lines.text: The chain lives on a flat floor with a pole going up. Mathematicians call the floor the complex plane. For us it is just a floor: so many steps right, so many steps back.
The pole is a dial. Its reading is called t. Turn it, and every joint in the chain bends.

chapters.title: Turn the Dial
chapters.subtitle: The tip keeps finding the centre

lines.text: Each joint bends by the dial reading times the log of its number. The straight chain curls into a spiral.
The chain is endless, so one orange arrow stands in for the whole rest of it.
lines.footnote: faint line: the next 120 arrows we do not draw · orange: Euler–Maclaurin tail N^(1−s)/(s−1) + N^−s/2 + Bernoulli terms

lines.text: Why is one arrow enough? The arrows we skip all turn at nearly the same rate, so together they trace a small, predictable curl: the faint line. Euler and Maclaurin's formula pins that curl down exactly, to a trillionth.
Now the tip is exact. Keep turning. The tip wanders, then dives straight into the centre.
At a dial reading of fourteen point one three it hits dead centre. We drop a marker on the pole at that height and call it a collision.
Twenty one. Twenty five. Thirty point four. The collisions never stop. In 1914 Hardy proved there are infinitely many on this pole; ten thousand are loaded here.
Here is the tip's whole path, threading the centre again and again. These collision heights are the famous zeros of the Riemann zeta function.
Start with an ordinary cosine wave, and a dial, gamma, that sets its speed.
Turn the dial up and the ripples pack tighter. The number inside the cosine is the only thing changing.
Now bend it. Put a logarithm inside, and the ripples bunch up near zero and widen as x grows.
Set the dial to the first collision height, fourteen point one three. This is the first collision's wave.
Take the second collision, twenty one point zero two, build its wave the same way, and add it on top. Watch the two merge: where they agree the peaks reinforce, where they disagree they cancel.
Keep going. The third wave. The fourth. Ten waves. Watch the pattern cancel itself out, wave by wave.
Hundreds of waves. What survives are sharp spikes, and they sit exactly on two, three, five, seven, eleven, thirteen, and the prime powers four, eight, nine.
A map of where the primes are, built from nothing but collision heights.
Riemann's exact recipe turns the map into a count. Start from the straight line y equals x, and subtract one weighted wave per collision.
Each weight is fixed by the recipe. Nothing is tuned by hand.
lines.footnote: ψ(x) = x − ln 2π − ½ ln(1 − x^-2) − 4√x Σ (cos(γ log x) + 2γ sin(γ log x)) / (1 + 4γ²)

lines.text: The result is a staircase. Every step is a prime: two, three, five, seven, eleven, thirteen. The red markers find them on their own.
More collisions, sharper steps. With a few hundred of them the staircase counts the primes exactly.
Now see it all at once. The chain shrinks by the square root rule. The dial turns. The tip strikes the centre, and every strike drops a marker on the pole.
Every marker becomes a wave, the waves pile up on the primes, and the staircase counts them. A machine for manufacturing prime numbers.

chapters.title: The Square-Root Key
chapters.subtitle: Why one half, and nothing else

lines.text: Back to the key. Everything used the square root: exponent one half. Change it to zero point nine and watch.
The spiral is tighter, and the tip never hits the centre. No collisions at all.
Picture every possible exponent between zero and one as a strip. Our collisions all sit on the one half line, right down the middle.
Suppose a collision strayed off that line, out to zero point nine. Its wave would grow like x to the zero point nine, and the staircase would wobble off the rails.
lines.footnote: red: the staircase if every collision had exponent 0.9 instead of ½

lines.text: The Riemann Hypothesis says it never happens: every collision, forever, exactly on the one half line. That is why the square root is the magic key.
In October 2026, OpenAI published an AI generated proof that no collision can stray past seven eighths. They call it the quasi Riemann hypothesis.
lines.footnote: openai/math, family 003 · manuscript Sept 30, 2026 · released Oct 6, 2026

lines.text: By symmetry, nothing below one eighth either. The blue bands are a wall: no collision can live there.
The core theorem is machine checked in Lean, and a companion proof reaches eleven twelfths. Human peer review is still under way, so call it a strong claim, not settled fact.
lines.footnote: Lean: riemannZeta s ≠ 0 for 7/8 < Re s · independently re-checked · not yet peer reviewed

lines.text: The orange gap, from one half out to seven eighths, is where the Riemann Hypothesis still lives. Push the wall all the way to one half, and the primes are finally tamed.
A chain that shrinks by the square root. A dial that turns. A tip that keeps striking the centre. And a staircase of primes that falls out of it.
Watch the spiral climb.
